recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A ragged collection of stars and gas clouds makes up the dwarf galaxy DDO 68 in this Hubble image. Astronomers call it an oddity.

At first glance it looks like a galaxy that formed only recently, right in our own galactic neighborhood. So the question is whether DDO 68 is really as young as it appears, or whether its youthful look is hiding an older past.

A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy, far less massive than the Milky Way, and dwarfs are thought to be some of the building blocks from which larger galaxies grow. That makes an unusual one like DDO 68 especially interesting to study. DDO 68 lies about 40 million light-years away in the constellation Leo. Hubble combined visible and near-infrared light with a filter that isolates glowing hydrogen gas, which traces regions where stars are forming.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.23 x 1.82 arcminutes) and distance (40 million light years), the frame spans roughly 38,000 × 21,000 light-years. Its light set out about 40 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using visible and near-infrared filters plus H-alpha for glowing hydrogen. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and this faint galaxy could not be seen this way without Hubble.
